1	\subsection{NG-33: check the mathematics returned by a reviewer}
2	\label{S:nogo-33}
3	
4	A review report is also a mathematical argument and can contain an incorrect
5	step. This historical record groups three such checks. The manuscript had
6	the correct expressions; the examples below explain why the proposed review
7	steps could not replace them. These are not three new counterexamples to the
8	stochastic model.
9	
10	\setcounter{nogo}{32}
11	\begin{nogo}[Three invalid proof steps]\label{P:nogo-33}
12	  The following assertions fail.
13	  \begin{enumerate}
14	    \item The free phase matrix
15	      $S_0(t)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
16	      is a contraction in the Euclidean norm for every $t\ge0$.
17	    \item For $0<\vartheta<1$, the series term $x^n/(n!)^\vartheta$ equals
18	      $A_nB_n$, where
19	      \[
20	        A_n=\frac{(2x^{1/\vartheta})^n}{n!},\qquad
21	        B_n=2^{-\vartheta n/(1-\vartheta)}.
22	      \]
23	    \item The denominator $k!\,k^{(2-\alpha)k}$ may always be replaced by
24	      the larger denominator $(k!)^3$ in the coefficient bound of
25	      Proposition~\ref{P:low-alpha-upper}.
26	  \end{enumerate}
27	\end{nogo}
28	
29	\begin{proof}
30	  The vector $(0,1)$ has norm one, but its image under $S_0(t)$ has norm
31	  $\sqrt{1+t^2}>1$ for $t>0$. To transfer this to the whole-space phase,
32	  use exactly the inhomogeneous Sobolev norm of
33	  Section~\ref{S:wave-variance}: $E=H^{1/2}\times H^{-1/2}$ and
34	  $J_0=\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda^{1/2},\Lambda^{-1/2})$, where
35	  $\Lambda=(1-\Delta)^{1/2}$. With $r=|\xi|$ and
36	  $\langle\xi\rangle=\sqrt{1+r^2}$, the Fourier symbol of
37	  $J_0S(t)J_0^{-1}$ is
38	  \[
39	    \begin{pmatrix}
40	      \cos(tr)&\langle\xi\rangle\sin(tr)/r\\
41	      -r\sin(tr)/\langle\xi\rangle&\cos(tr)
42	    \end{pmatrix}
43	    \longrightarrow S_0(t)\qquad(r\downarrow0).
44	  \]
45	  Choose normalized Fourier bumps supported in balls shrinking to zero
46	  and place them in the second coordinate of $J_0z$. Continuity of this
47	  matrix at zero shows that their image norms tend to $\sqrt{1+t^2}$.
48	  Thus $S(t)$ is not a contraction on this $E$. The distinction between
49	  $\langle\xi\rangle$ and $|\xi|$ matters: this is not a claim about the
50	  homogeneous energy norm. The valid estimate keeps a free-growth factor.
51	
52	  The correct identity in the second assertion is
53	  $x^n/(n!)^\vartheta=A_n^\vartheta B_n^{1-\vartheta}$.
54	  At $\vartheta=3/4$, $n=1$ and $x=1$, its left side is one, whereas
55	  $A_1B_1=2\cdot(1/8)=1/4$. H\"older applies to the weighted product, as
56	  in the proof of Proposition~\ref{P:static-phase-all-orders}.
57	
58	  For the third assertion choose the permitted spatial-white value
59	  $\alpha=1$ and $k=3$. Then $k!k^{(2-\alpha)k}=162<216=(k!)^3$.
60	  An upper bound $M/162$ does not imply the smaller upper bound $M/216$.
61	  The valid factorial weakening is instead
62	  \[
63	    k!k^{(2-\alpha)k}\ge(k!)^{3-\alpha},
64	  \]
65	  since $k!\le k^k$ and $2-\alpha>0$; at this example its right side is
66	  $36$. This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-33}.
67	\end{proof}
68	
69	\paragraph{Scope and what survives.}
70	The last arithmetic check refutes an inference between numerical bounds;
71	it does not prove that the actual coefficient exceeds $M/216$.
72	All three corrected arguments remain in the main text. Their lesson is to
73	check an asserted derivation against its domains, factors and quantifiers,
74	even when the report containing it has a favorable overall verdict.
75	
76	\paragraph{What would permit the discarded steps?}
77	Contractivity needs a suitable invariant norm or a restricted state class.
78	The H\"older factors need their conjugate powers. A stronger factorial
79	bound needs an additional estimate; it cannot be obtained by changing the
80	exponent in the denominator.

1	# Exact phase and unitary normalization
2	\subsection{Forms on the full phase}
3	
4	Choose and fix $T > 0$. Set $\Lambda = (1-\Delta)^{1/2}$, $s = 1/2$ and $E_r =
5	H^r(\R^d)\times H^{r-1}(\R^d)$. On the complexification of $E = E_s$, use inner
6	products linear in the first slot. The map
7	\[
8	  Jz(\xi) = \left(\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}\widehat{z}_1(\xi),
9	  \langle\xi\rangle^{-1/2}\widehat{z}_2(\xi)\right)
10	\]
11	is unitary onto $L^2(\R^d;\mathbb{C}^2)$. The full massless wave group has
12	Fourier matrix
13	\begin{equation}\label{E:variance-free-matrix}
14	  S(t,\xi) =
15	  \begin{pmatrix}
16	    \cos(t|\xi|) & \sin(t|\xi|)/|\xi|\\
17	    -|\xi|\sin(t|\xi|) & \cos(t|\xi|)
18	  \end{pmatrix},
19	\end{equation}
20	where the sine quotient is $t$ at zero. Let $B(b)(u,v) = (0,bu)$. Choose and fix
21	a real even nonnegative $\zeta \in C_c^\infty(\R^d)$ equal to one on $B_1$ and
22	zero off $B_2$, and put $\zeta_R(x) = \zeta(x/R)$ for $R > 0$. For $I =
23	[t_0,t_0+h] \subset [0,T]$, $0 < h \le 1$, and Schwartz phases $z,w$, put
24	\begin{align}
25	  v_z(t) &= [S(t)z]_1,
26	  \label{E:variance-displacement}\\
27	  G_w(t) &= -\frac{\sin(t|D|)}{|D|}\Lambda w_1
28	  +\cos(t|D|)\Lambda^{-1}w_2,
29	  \label{E:variance-dual-wave}\\
30	  F_{z,w}(t,x) &= 1_I(t)v_z(t,x)\overline{G_w(t,x)},
31	  \qquad \ell_R(I;z,w) = W_{\mathbb{C}}(\zeta_RF_{z,w}),
32	  \label{E:variance-actual-form}
33	\end{align}
34	where $W_{\mathbb{C}}(F) = W(\operatorname{Re}F)+iW(\operatorname{Im}F)$. There
35	is no observation cutoff in this definition.
36	
37	We first assume $\Gamma \ne 0$. If $\Gamma = 0$, all forms and the column maps
38	below are zero, so their bounds hold directly. For the nonzero case, let $\nu_R$
39	be~\eqref{E:masked-auxiliary-measure} and set
40	\begin{equation}\label{E:variance-actual-growth-constant}
41	  L_\zeta = \|\widehat{\zeta}\|_1,\qquad
42	  C_\nu = c_d^2L_\zeta^2C_\Gamma.
43	\end{equation}
44	Proposition~\ref{P:masked-auxiliary-norm} gives a positive even tempered Radon
45	measure with $\nu_R(B(y,r)) \le C_\nu r^\alpha$, uniformly in $R$.

48	# P:low-alpha-upper
49	\begin{proposition}[Upper bound for $\alpha \le 1$]\label{P:low-alpha-upper}
50	  Suppose that Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} and the standing covariance positivity
51	  assumptions hold, $d \in \{1,2,3\}$, $0 < \alpha \le 1$, and $V > 0$. Define
52	  \begin{equation}\label{E:low-alpha-constants}
53	    \begin{split}
54	      K_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen}
55	      &=\begin{cases}
56	        \displaystyle\frac{V2^{2-\alpha}(1-\alpha)^{-\alpha}}
57	        {(2-\alpha)^{2-\alpha}},&0<\alpha<1,\\[2mm]
58	        \pi V,&\alpha=1,
59	      \end{cases}\\
60	      C_2^{\rm gen}&=q(2ZK_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen})^{1/q}.
61	    \end{split}
62	  \end{equation}
63	  With the same $A_k$, $b$, $q$, $\beta$, and $Z$ as above, for
64	  $k \ge 1$ and $t > 0$,
65	  \begin{equation}\label{E:low-alpha-coefficient}
66	    A_k(t)\le\frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen})^k t^{\beta k}}
67	    {k!\,k^{bk}}
68	    \le\frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen})^k t^{\beta k}}{(k!)^q},
69	    \qquad
70	    \E u^2(t,x)\le\exp(C_2^{\rm gen}t^\kappa).
71	  \end{equation}
72	\end{proposition}
73	
74	\begin{proof}
75	  First smooth the noise as in~\cite{chen:author2026:time-dependency}*{(2.9), (2.11), (2.23)--(2.24)}.
76	  In dimension three also use $G_{h,\eta}$ with $\eta > 0$, as in the
77	  source's pp.~13--14. The increment change of variables is now a
78	  triangular map on vectors in $\R^d$, still of determinant one.
79	  The descending-label proof of Lemma~\ref{L:d1-spatial} depends only
80	  on which increments enter each position, not on their dimension.
81	  Its invariant therefore remains valid: at a closing label there
82	  is exactly one covariance depending on that vector increment, and
83	  at an opening label its pair has already been removed.
84	  If $0 < \alpha < 1$, Lemma~\ref{L:low-alpha-convolution} gives the
85	  closing bound $Mh_l^{1-\alpha}$ with $M = V/(1-\alpha)$.
86	  At $\alpha = 1$, Lemma~\ref{L:alpha-one-convolution} gives the
87	  constant closing bound $M = \pi V/2$. Every opening gives mass
88	  $h_l$, uniformly in $\eta$ and all noise-smoothing parameters.
89	  For $\alpha < 1$, the same weighted arithmetic--geometric mean
90	  calculation gives
91	  \[
92	    M^k\prod_{i\in O_D}h_i\prod_{j\in C_D}h_j^{1-\alpha}
93	    \le (K_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen})^k\frac{t^{bk}}{k^{bk}}.
94	  \]
95	  At $\alpha = 1$, ordinary arithmetic--geometric mean on the $k$ opening
96	  increments gives $M^k\prod_{i\in O_D}h_i \le (2M)^kt^k/k^k$, which is the same
97	  bound with $b = 1$ and $K_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen} = \pi V$. Both cases use
98	  $\sum_lh_l \le 2t$. For $d = 1,2$ one may use the Green densities directly;
99	  their opening mass and closing convolution obey these same bounds.
100	
101	  Replace the nonnegative truncated temporal factors by $|s_i-s_j|^{-\alpha_0}$
102	  before taking their pairing sum. The temporal symmetry, cube integral and
103	  split count in~\eqref{E:d1-time-symmetry} do not involve the spatial
104	  dimension. Thus, exactly the multiplication of counts in the proof of
105	  Proposition~\ref{P:d1-upper} gives the first bound
106	  in~\eqref{E:low-alpha-coefficient} for the regularized moments.
107	
108	  We spell out the limit in dimension three. Fix every noise-smoothing parameter
109	  and first let $\eta\downarrow0$. At each time vector, the Gaussian moment
110	  formula is a finite sum of bounded continuous products of the smoothed
111	  covariance functions, integrated against products of the finite Green
112	  measures. These products of measures converge weakly as $\eta\downarrow0$,
113	  with the same masses $\prod_l h_l$. At fixed noise smoothing the Gaussian
114	  covariance factors are uniformly bounded, so a constant times $\prod_lh_l$
115	  dominates on each bounded time simplex. Dominated convergence applies also to
116	  the covariance between two approximations with different $\eta$ values. The
117	  resulting common joint covariance limit proves the $L^2$ Cauchy property of
118	  each fixed-order random integral. This is the inner limit used in the source's
119	  definition on pp.~13--14. Products of two factors converge in $L^1$ by
120	  Cauchy--Schwarz, so the moment inequality survives this limit. Next send the
121	  noise-smoothing parameters to zero using the fixed-order $L^2$ convergence of
122	  Lemma~\ref{L:joint-fixed-order}, and again pass products in $L^1$. In
123	  dimensions one and two only the latter limit is required. The bounds at both
124	  stages are uniform.
125	
126	  We have proved the first coefficient bound for $A_k(t)$. The factorial
127	  inequality and nonnegative-series argument in Proposition~\ref{P:d1-upper}
128	  apply unchanged, with $K_{\rm sp}^{\rm gen}$ in place of $K_{\rm sp}$ and $A_0
129	  = 1$. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:low-alpha-upper}.
130	\end{proof}
131	# P:static-phase-all-orders
132	\begin{proposition}[All regularized static phase orders]
133	  \label{P:static-phase-all-orders}
134	  Retain the full covariance class of Section~\ref{S:static-phase}. For real
135	  Schwartz $f,g$, let $Z_n^\epsilon(h)$ be the $n$th regularized static Duhamel
136	  phase, with the recursion \eqref{E:phase-duhamel} for every $n \ge 0$. This is
137	  an ordinary Gaussian polynomial of degree at most $n$, including
138	  self-contractions; it is not a pure Wick chaos. There is an explicit finite
139	  constant
140	  \[
141	    A_\alpha=\frac{400\sqrt2\,e^2}{\delta_{\alpha/2}}
142	  \]
143	  such that, for $n \ge 1$, uniformly in $\epsilon > 0$,
144	  \begin{equation}\label{E:all-static-phase-orders}
145	    \|Z_n^\epsilon(h)\|_{L^2(\Omega;X_{1/h})}
146	    \le
147	    \frac{(A_\alpha\sqrt{R_\alpha})^n
148	    h^{(4-\alpha)n/2}}{(n!)^{(3-\alpha)/2}}
149	    \|(f,g)\|_{1/h}.
150	  \end{equation}
151	  At every fixed positive smoothing and real coupling $\sigma$,
152	  $\sum_{n\ge0}\sigma^nZ_n^\epsilon(h)$ converges in $L^2$ phase. Its squared
153	  norm is at most
154	  \begin{equation}\label{E:all-static-phase-sum}
155	    (\sqrt e+2)^2
156	    \exp\left\{6A_\alpha^{2/(3-\alpha)}
157	    (|\sigma|^2R_\alpha)^{1/(3-\alpha)}
158	    h^{(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha)}\right\}\|(f,g)\|_{1/h}^2.
159	  \end{equation}
160	\end{proposition}
161	
162	\begin{proof}
163	  If $R_\alpha = 0$, spectral homogeneity gives $\mu = 0$, and every
164	  positive-order term is zero. Assume $R_\alpha > 0$. First work at finite
165	  Gaussian cutoff $m$, degree cutoff $N$ and spatial band $b$, with initial
166	  phase $S_b(f,g)$ times the Gaussian vacuum $1$. All relevant operators are
167	  bounded. Lemmas~\ref{L:fock-form} and~\ref{L:complex-phase}, with $a =
168	  \alpha/2$, give a bound $100e^{2\lambda h}$ on the complex coupling circle of
169	  radius $\delta_{\alpha/2}\lambda^{2-\alpha/2}/d_N$.
170	
171	  The four phase entries are entire in the coupling, by the power series for
172	  $\cos(h\sqrt L)$ and $\sin(h\sqrt L)/\sqrt L$ of a bounded $L$. Cauchy's
173	  formula for their operator-valued series bounds the $n$th coefficient by
174	  \[
175	    100e^{2\lambda h}
176	    \left(\frac{d_N}
177	    {\delta_{\alpha/2}\lambda^{2-\alpha/2}}\right)^n
178	    \|S_b(f,g)\|_\lambda .
179	  \]
180	  The coefficient is exactly the $n$th Duhamel phase from the vacuum. Apply
181	  Lemma~\ref{L:finite-word-cutoff} with one color, $N = n$, the spatial phase
182	  Hilbert space as $\mathscr{X}$, and its free wave operators as the $F_l$. It
183	  identifies each cutoff Duhamel word exactly with its uncompressed word,
184	  including self-contractions. Dominated time integration preserves this
185	  identity.
186	
187	  Choose $\lambda = n/h$. For any phase $z$, $\|z\|_{1/h} \le n\|z\|_{n/h}$ and
188	  $\|(f,g)\|_{n/h} \le \|(f,g)\|_{1/h}$. Also $d_n \le
189	  2\sqrt{2n}\sqrt{R_\alpha}$. The preceding bound is therefore at most
190	  \[
191	    100n\left(\frac{2\sqrt2 e^2}{\delta_{\alpha/2}}\right)^n
192	    R_\alpha^{n/2}h^{(4-\alpha)n/2}
193	    n^{-(3-\alpha)n/2}\|(f,g)\|_{1/h}.
194	  \]
195	  Since $100n \le 200^n$ and $n! \le n^n$, this gives
196	  \eqref{E:all-static-phase-orders} at the cutoffs.
197	
198	  We justify removal of those cutoffs at fixed $\epsilon$ and $n$. On Gaussian
199	  degrees at most $N$, the unweighted field multiplication has norm at most
200	  $2\sqrt{N+1}\sqrt{v_\epsilon}$, uniformly in $m$, by the same
201	  creation/annihilation argument applied pointwise in $x$. It follows that the
202	  noise phase insertion $(u,v)\mapsto(0,W_\epsilon u)$, between the required
203	  finite degree levels, is bounded on $X_\lambda$ by this constant divided by
204	  $\lambda$. Free phase evolution is bounded by $e^{\lambda h/2}$. For finite
205	  $m$, $S_b \to I$ strongly and commutes with the free propagator. Each fixed
206	  Duhamel word therefore converges strongly as $b \to \infty$, by dominated time
207	  integration.
208	
209	  Next let $m \to \infty$ on the full Gaussian space. The truncated field
210	  multiplications converge strongly between finite degree levels. To see this,
211	  first take a vector depending on finitely many Gaussian coordinates. The
212	  annihilation tail is then zero, while the creation tail is bounded by a
213	  constant times
214	  \[
215	    \left(\int\sum_{i>m}e_i(x)^2\|F(x)\|^2\ud x\right)^{1/2},
216	  \]
217	  which tends to zero by dominated convergence, since the sum is bounded by
218	  $v_\epsilon$. Such vectors are dense; the uniform multiplication bound extends
219	  strong convergence to all vectors in those degree levels. Dominated time
220	  integration again gives convergence of every fixed word. The limit is
221	  precisely $Z_n^\epsilon$, so the estimate survives both limits. We assert no
222	  zero-smoothing phase limit in this argument.
223	
224	  Finally, put $\beta = (3-\alpha)/2 \in (1/2,3/2)$ and $x =
225	  A_\alpha|\sigma|\sqrt{R_\alpha}h^{(4-\alpha)/2}$. The elementary series
226	  satisfies
227	  \[
228	    \sum_{n\ge0}\frac{x^n}{(n!)^\beta}
229	    \le2e^{3x^{1/\beta}}.
230	  \]
231	  For $\beta \ge 1$, this follows from $\sum a_n^\beta \le (\sum a_n)^\beta$
232	  with $a_n = x^{n/\beta}/n!$. For $\beta < 1$, apply H\"older to
233	  $((2x^{1/\beta})^n/n!)^\beta (2^{-\beta n/(1-\beta)})^{1-\beta}$. The second
234	  geometric sum is at most two. Since $\|Z_0(h)\|_{1/h} \le \sqrt
235	  e\|(f,g)\|_{1/h}$, absolute $L^2$ summation and squaring give
236	  \eqref{E:all-static-phase-sum}. This proves
237	  Proposition~\ref{P:static-phase-all-orders}.
238	\end{proof}
239	# Complete direct-bound section, including b=2-alpha and upstream convolution lemmas
240	\section{Upper bounds for spatial exponents at most one}\label{S:d1-upper}
241	
242	The upper bound at scale $t^\kappa$ is proved for $0 < \alpha \le 1$ in
243	dimensions one, two and three under the standing assumptions. The separate
244	one-dimensional Riesz estimates retain their sharper constants and white
245	endpoint. Degree-one covariance in dimensions two and three does not mean full
246	spatial white noise. Section~\ref{S:interval-upper} treats the higher exponents
247	by a separate argument. The intrinsic constant is identified  in
248	Theorem~\ref{T:intrinsic-second-moment}.
249	
250	We retain the two-chain expansion of Proposition~\ref{P:mixed}, but estimate its
251	spatial and temporal factors in a different order. The spatial estimate keeps a
252	power of the number of pairs. After taking a common spatial maximum, we sum all
253	temporal pairings before using the ordered time domains.
254	
255	Throughout this section $0 < \alpha_0 < 1$. We first work in dimension one with
256	either of the spatial covariances
257	\begin{equation}\label{E:d1-covariances}
258	  \begin{cases}
259	    \gamma(y)=c_\alpha|y|^{-\alpha},&0<\alpha<1,\quad c_\alpha>0,\\
260	    \gamma=c_\delta\delta_0,&\alpha=1,\quad c_\delta>0.
261	  \end{cases}
262	\end{equation}
263	Put $b = 2-\alpha$, $q = 3-\alpha$, $\beta = 4-\alpha-\alpha_0$, and
264	\begin{equation}\label{E:d1-constants}
265	  Z=\frac{2}{(1-\alpha_0)(2-\alpha_0)},\qquad
266	  K_{\rm sp}=
267	  \begin{cases}
268	    \displaystyle\frac{c_\alpha 2^{2-\alpha}(1-\alpha)^{-\alpha}}
269	    {(2-\alpha)^{2-\alpha}},&0<\alpha<1,\\[2mm]
270	    c_\delta,&\alpha=1.
271	  \end{cases}
272	\end{equation}
273	These parameters satisfy Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, so the fixed-order
274	integrability and mixed expansion already established apply.
275	
276	\subsection{A spatial bound retaining the ordered increments}
277	
278	For $m+n = 2k$, label the two chains in block order as in~\eqref{E:mixed-diagram}. For each vertex $l$ write
279	$h_l = s_l-s_{p(l)} > 0$ and $y_l = x_l-x_{p(l)}$, with a separate root zero
280	in each chain. Thus, $x_l$ is the sum of increments in its own chain
281	up to label $l$. The spatial change of variables has determinant one.
282	In this section $x_l$ denotes a spatial position and $y_l$ its increment; this local
283	notation differs from the position variables $y_l$
284	in~\eqref{E:mixed-diagram}. The terminal evaluation point of $u(t,x)$
285	remains denoted by $x$.
286	Let $p_\epsilon$ be the centered Brownian Gaussian density of variance
287	$\epsilon$ and mass one, and set
288	$\gamma_\epsilon = p_\epsilon*\gamma$. Allow a separate positive
289	$\epsilon_e$ for every pair $e \in D$ and define
290	\[
291	  S_{D,\boldsymbol\epsilon}(h)
292	  =\int_{\R^{2k}}\prod_{l=1}^{2k}G(h_l,y_l)
293	  \prod_{(i,j)\in D}\gamma_{\epsilon_{i,j}}(x_j-x_i)\ud y,
294	  \qquad G(h,y)=\tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{|y|<h\}}.
295	\]
296	This is an ordinary nonnegative integral; no pointwise delta value is used.
297	
298	\begin{lemma}[Spatial estimate]\label{L:d1-spatial}
299	  Suppose~\eqref{E:d1-covariances} holds, $k \ge 1$, and $D$ is any pairing of
300	  the two chains. Orient every pair $(i,j)$ by $i < j$ and let $O_D$ and $C_D$
301	  be its opening and closing label sets. Then, uniformly in
302	  $\boldsymbol\epsilon$,
303	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-spatial-product}
304	    S_{D,\boldsymbol\epsilon}(h)\le
305	    \begin{cases}
306	      \displaystyle\left(\frac{c_\alpha}{1-\alpha}\right)^k
307	      \prod_{i\in O_D}h_i\prod_{j\in C_D}h_j^{1-\alpha},
308	      &0<\alpha<1,\\[2mm]
309	      \displaystyle\left(\frac{c_\delta}{2}\right)^k
310	      \prod_{i\in O_D}h_i,&\alpha=1.
311	    \end{cases}
312	  \end{equation}
313	  In particular, if $\sum_{l=1}^{2k}h_l \le 2t$, then
314	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-spatial-max}
315	    S_{D,\boldsymbol\epsilon}(h)
316	    \le K_{\rm sp}^{\,k}\frac{t^{bk}}{k^{bk}}.
317	  \end{equation}
318	\end{lemma}
319	
320	\begin{proof}
321	  We first record the convolution bounds. For $0 < \alpha < 1$, the
322	  integral of the even decreasing function $|y|^{-\alpha}$ over an
323	  interval of fixed length is maximal when the interval is centered
324	  at zero. Therefore,
325	  \[
326	    \sup_z\int_\R G(h,y)c_\alpha|y+z|^{-\alpha}\ud y
327	    =\frac{c_\alpha h^{1-\alpha}}{1-\alpha}.
328	  \]
329	  By Tonelli's theorem, the integral with $\gamma_\epsilon$ equals the
330	  $p_\epsilon(w)\ud w$ average of the unsmoothed integrals with shifts $z-w$.
331	  Its nonnegative mass-one average is therefore bounded by the same supremum. In
332	  the white case, $\gamma_\epsilon = c_\delta p_\epsilon$, so
333	  \[
334	    \sup_z\int_\R G(h,y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)\ud y
335	    \le\frac{c_\delta}{2}.
336	  \]
337	  Both estimates are uniform in $\epsilon > 0$.
338	
339	  Now integrate \emph{all} spatial increments in descending label order
340	  $2k,2k-1,\ldots,1$. Before processing label $l$, the remaining covariance
341	  factors are exactly those pairs whose closing labels are at most $l$; the
342	  bounds from the removed pairs depend only on $h$. If $l \in C_D$, its pair is
343	  $(i,l)$ with $i < l$ and $x_l-x_i = y_l+z$, where $z$ is independent of $y_l$.
344	  Every other remaining pair has both endpoints smaller than $l$, so its two
345	  positions are independent of $y_l$: positions involve only earlier increments
346	  in their own block chain. Thus, the only covariance involving $y_l$ is its own
347	  pair, and the convolution bound removes it. If $l \in O_D$, its partner has a
348	  larger label and its covariance factor has already been removed. All remaining
349	  covariances have endpoints smaller than $l$, so integration of $y_l$ gives

369	\subsection{Summing temporal pairings before using time ordering}
370	
371	Define the total-order coefficients
372	\[
373	  A_k(t)=\sum_{m=0}^{2k}\E[X_m(t,x)X_{2k-m}(t,x)],\qquad A_0(t)=1.
374	\]
375	They do not depend on $x$, by spatial stationarity. By
376	Proposition~\ref{P:mixed}, $\E u^2(t,x) = \sum_{k\ge0}A_k(t)$.
377	
378	\begin{proposition}[One-dimensional upper bound]\label{P:d1-upper}
379	  Under~\eqref{E:d1-covariances}, for every $k \ge 1$ and $t > 0$,
380	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-coefficient}
381	    A_k(t)\le
382	    \frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp})^k t^{\beta k}}{k!\,k^{bk}}
383	    \le\frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp})^k t^{\beta k}}{(k!)^q}.
384	  \end{equation}
385	  Consequently,
386	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-upper}
387	    \E u^2(t,x)\le\exp(C_2t^\kappa),\qquad
388	    C_2=q(2ZK_{\rm sp})^{1/q},\quad \kappa=\frac{\beta}{q}.
389	  \end{equation}
390	\end{proposition}
391	
392	\begin{proof}
393	  We first work with the Gaussian spatial smoothing and temporal truncation
394	  in~\cite{chen:author2026:time-dependency}*{(2.9), (2.11), (2.23)--(2.24)}. Let
395	  $X_n^{\epsilon,\delta}$ be the smoothed Stratonovich term, using common
396	  parameters in every factor. Wick's formula expresses each mixed expectation of
397	  total order $2k$ as a sum over $D \in \Pi_k$. After the chain reversal in
398	  Proposition~\ref{P:mixed}, its spatial factor is the one in
399	  Lemma~\ref{L:d1-spatial}; its temporal factors are nonnegative and bounded by
400	  $|s_i-s_j|^{-\alpha_0}$. For times in $[0,t]^m_ < \times[0,t]^{2k-m}_ <$, the
401	  increments sum to the two terminal times and therefore to at most $2t$.
402	  Extract~\eqref{E:d1-spatial-max}, which is independent of the time vector, the
403	  split, the pairing, and the smoothing parameters. The remaining temporal sum
404	  is
405	  \[
406	    F_k(s_1,\ldots,s_{2k})
407	    =\sum_{D\in\Pi_k}\prod_{(i,j)\in D}|s_i-s_j|^{-\alpha_0}.
408	  \]
409	  Every permutation of the $2k$ labels bijects $\Pi_k$, so $F_k$ is fully
410	  symmetric. Moreover,
411	  \[
412	    \int_{[0,t]^2}|s-r|^{-\alpha_0}\ud s\ud r
413	    =Zt^{2-\alpha_0},\qquad
414	    \int_{[0,t]^{2k}}F_k(s)\ud s
415	    =P_k(Zt^{2-\alpha_0})^k<\infty.
416	  \]
417	  The second equality uses the disjoint endpoints of every pairing. Partitioning
418	  the time cube according to the order within each block now gives
419	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-time-symmetry}
420	    \int_{[0,t]^m_<\times[0,t]^{2k-m}_<}F_k(s)\ud s
421	    =\frac{P_k(Zt^{2-\alpha_0})^k}{m!(2k-m)!}.
422	  \end{equation}
423	  Ties have measure zero. Crucially, this symmetry is applied to the \emph{sum}
424	  of pairings after taking the common spatial bound, not to an individual
425	  temporally weighted diagram.
426	
427	  The number of pairings obeys $P_0 = 1$ and $P_k = (2k-1)P_{k-1}$, by choosing
428	  the partner of the smallest label. Hence, $P_k = (2k)!/(2^kk!)$. The binomial
429	  identity gives
430	  \[
431	    \sum_{m=0}^{2k}\frac1{m!(2k-m)!}=\frac{2^{2k}}{(2k)!}.
432	  \]
433	  Multiplying~\eqref{E:d1-time-symmetry} by the spatial bound and summing over
434	  $m$ yields
435	  \[
436	    \sum_{m=0}^{2k}\E[X_m^{\epsilon,\delta}X_{2k-m}^{\epsilon,\delta}]
437	    \le K_{\rm sp}^{\,k}\frac{t^{bk}}{k^{bk}}
438	    \frac{2^{2k}}{(2k)!}
439	    \frac{(2k)!}{2^kk!}(Zt^{2-\alpha_0})^k
440	    =\frac{(2ZK_{\rm sp})^kt^{\beta k}}{k!\,k^{bk}}.
441	  \]
442	  The same proof covers empty chains, with $X_0^{\epsilon,\delta} = 1$.
443	
444	  By Lemma~\ref{L:joint-fixed-order}, each smoothed factor converges in $L^2$.
445	  Products converge in $L^1$ by Cauchy--Schwarz; for fixed $k$ the sum over
446	  splits is finite. The bound is uniform in $\epsilon,\delta$, so it passes to
447	  $A_k(t)$. Since $k! \le k^k$ and $b > 0$, we have $k!\,k^{bk} \ge (k!)^{b+1} =
448	  (k!)^q$, proving both inequalities in~\eqref{E:d1-coefficient}.
449	
450	  Finally, for $z \ge 0$ and $q \ge 1$,
451	  \[
452	    \sum_{k\ge0}\frac{z^k}{(k!)^q}
453	    =\sum_{k\ge0}\left(\frac{z^{k/q}}{k!}\right)^q
454	    \le\left(\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{z^{k/q}}{k!}\right)^q
455	    =\exp(qz^{1/q}).
456	  \]
457	  Apply this inequality with $z = 2ZK_{\rm sp}t^\beta$, adding the separately
458	  defined term $A_0 = 1$. Proposition~\ref{P:mixed} then
459	  gives~\eqref{E:d1-upper}. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:d1-upper}.
460	\end{proof}

462	\subsection{Spectral bounds for $0 < \alpha \le 1$ in all three dimensions}
463	
464	We now retain Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} with $d \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $0 < \alpha
465	\le 1$. The covariance is nonnegative and nonnegative definite as in
466	Section~\ref{S:model}; when it is a distribution, both these properties and its
467	homogeneity are understood distributionally. Let $\mu$ be its positive Radon
468	spectral measure in the convention $\gamma(x) = \int e^{i\xi\cdot
469	x}\mu(\ud\xi)$, and put $V = \mu(\{\xi:|\xi|\le1\})$. No isotropy or spectral
470	density is assumed. Write $G_h$ for the positive wave-kernel measure of mass
471	$h$, and $G_{h,\eta} = p_\eta*G_h$ for $\eta > 0$; set $G_{h,0} = G_h$. The
472	measure notation includes the sphere kernel in dimension three. The mixed-moment
473	definition of $A_k(t)$ is now applied to the present $d$-dimensional solution.

475	\begin{lemma}[Low-$\alpha$ convolution bound]\label{L:low-alpha-convolution}
476	  Under the preceding assumptions with $0 < \alpha < 1$, for every $R,h > 0$,
477	  \begin{equation}\label{E:low-alpha-radial}
478	    \mu(\{\xi:|\xi|\le R\})=VR^\alpha,\qquad
479	    \int_{\R^d}\min\{h,|\xi|^{-1}\}\mu(\ud\xi)
480	    =\frac{V}{1-\alpha}h^{1-\alpha}.
481	  \end{equation}
482	  For $\epsilon > 0$ and $\eta \ge 0$,
483	  \begin{equation}\label{E:low-alpha-convolution}
484	    0\le\int_{\R^d}G_{h,\eta}(\ud y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)
485	    \le\frac{V}{1-\alpha}h^{1-\alpha},
486	    \qquad z\in\R^d.
487	  \end{equation}
488	  The estimate is uniform in both smoothing parameters and in $z$.
489	\end{lemma}
490	
491	\begin{proof}
492	  The spectral measure of $\gamma(c\,\cdot)$ is the pushforward of $\mu$ under
493	  $\xi\mapsto c\xi$. Homogeneity and uniqueness of the Fourier transform on
494	  tempered distributions therefore give $\mu(A/c) = c^{-\alpha}\mu(A)$ for every
495	  Borel set $A$. Equivalently, $\mu(cA) = c^\alpha\mu(A)$. This proves the
496	  ball-mass formula. Since $\mu$ is Radon, $V < \infty$, and continuity from
497	  above gives $\mu(\{0\}) = \lim_{R\downarrow0}VR^\alpha = 0$. By the layer-cake
498	  identity and Tonelli's theorem,
499	  \[
500	    \int_{\R^d}\min\{h,|\xi|^{-1}\}\mu(\ud\xi)
501	    =\int_0^h\mu(\{\xi:|\xi|\le u^{-1}\})\ud u
502	    =V\int_0^h u^{-\alpha}\ud u.
503	  \]
504	  The endpoint of each indicator has no effect on its $u$ integral. Since
505	  $\alpha < 1$, the last expression is the finite quantity
506	  in~\eqref{E:low-alpha-radial}. This computation uses ball masses, not a radial
507	  density for $\mu$.
508	
509	  Gaussian weighting gives a finite measure, by the polynomial ball growth of
510	  $\mu$. Thus, Fourier Fubini is justified for $\gamma_\epsilon$ and the finite
511	  measure $G_{h,\eta}$. From the source's wave-kernel
512	  formulas~\cite{chen:author2026:time-dependency}*{(2.3)--(2.5), p.~7},
513	  \[
514	    \widehat{G}_h(\xi)=\frac{\sin(h|\xi|)}{|\xi|},\qquad
515	    G_h(\R^d)=h,
516	  \]
517	  with value $h$ in the Fourier formula at zero. The Fourier multipliers of
518	  $p_\epsilon$ and $p_\eta$ have absolute value at most one, with the latter
519	  multiplier equal to one when $\eta = 0$. Consequently,
520	  \[
521	    \left|\int G_{h,\eta}(\ud y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)\right|
522	    \le\int_{\R^d}\frac{|\sin(h|\xi|)|}{|\xi|}\mu(\ud\xi)
523	    \le\int_{\R^d}\min\{h,|\xi|^{-1}\}\mu(\ud\xi).
524	  \]
525	  Nonnegativity of $\gamma$ as a distribution implies $\gamma_\epsilon \ge 0$,
526	  since Gaussian translates are nonnegative test functions; $G_{h,\eta}$ is also
527	  nonnegative. This proves the lower bound in~\eqref{E:low-alpha-convolution}.
528	  Combining the preceding displays proves its upper bound. No positivity of the
529	  oscillatory Fourier integrand is asserted. This proves
530	  Lemma~\ref{L:low-alpha-convolution}.
531	\end{proof}

533	\begin{lemma}[Degree-one convolution bound]\label{L:alpha-one-convolution}
534	  Under the preceding covariance assumptions with $\alpha = 1$, for every $h >
535	  0$, $\epsilon > 0$, $\eta \ge 0$, and $z \in \R^d$,
536	  \begin{equation}\label{E:alpha-one-convolution}
537	    0\le\int_{\R^d}G_{h,\eta}(\ud y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)
538	    \le\frac{\pi V}{2}.
539	  \end{equation}
540	  No isotropy or angular density is required.
541	\end{lemma}
542	
543	\begin{proof}
544	  Fourier uniqueness, applied to the distributional homogeneity as above, gives
545	  $\mu(cA) = c\mu(A)$ and $\mu(\{0\}) = 0$. Define a finite measure on the unit
546	  sphere by
547	  \[
548	    \sigma(E)=\mu\{\xi:0<|\xi|\le1,\ \xi/|\xi|\in E\}.
549	  \]
550	  Its total mass is $V$. Homogeneity implies that the corresponding sector of
551	  radius $R$ has mass $R\sigma(E)$. Subtracting two such sectors shows that a
552	  polar rectangle $(r_1,r_2]\times E$ has mass $(r_2-r_1)\sigma(E)$. Uniqueness
553	  of measures on these generating rectangles therefore gives the polar
554	  decomposition $\mu(\ud\xi) = \ud r\,\sigma(\ud\theta)$, $r > 0$, $\theta \in
555	  \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. The real stationary covariance is even; Fourier uniqueness
556	  makes $\mu$, and hence $\sigma$, even.
557	
558	  Use the Brownian Gaussian convention, so the combined covariance and Green
559	  smoothing multiplier is $e^{-ar^2}$ with $a = (\epsilon+\eta)/2 > 0$. Gaussian
560	  weighting makes the spectral measure finite. Fourier Fubini and evenness give
561	  \begin{equation}\label{E:alpha-one-polar}
562	    \begin{split}
563	      \int G_{h,\eta}(\ud y)\gamma_\epsilon(y+z)
564	      &=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} I_a(h,\theta\cdot z)\sigma(\ud\theta),\\
565	      I_a(h,v)&=\int_0^\infty e^{-ar^2}
566	      \frac{\sin(hr)}r\cos(rv)\ud r.
567	    \end{split}
568	  \end{equation}
569	  The radial integral is absolutely convergent: its integrand is bounded near
570	  zero and Gaussian-decaying at infinity. Passing from the complex exponential
571	  to cosine introduces no factor two, since both antipodal directions are
572	  already included in $\sigma$.
573	
574	  Let $g_h(v) = \tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{|v|<h\}}$ and let $p_{2a}^{(1)}(v) = (4\pi
575	  a)^{-1/2}e^{-v^2/(4a)}$ be the one-dimensional Gaussian density. Their Fourier
576	  transforms are $\sin(hr)/r$ and $e^{-ar^2}$. The one-dimensional inversion
577	  factor is $1/(2\pi)$ in the source convention, so
578	  \[
579	    (g_h*p_{2a}^{(1)})(v)
580	    =\frac1{2\pi}\int_\R e^{irv}e^{-ar^2}
581	    \frac{\sin(hr)}r\ud r
582	    =\frac1\pi I_a(h,v).
583	  \]
584	  The sign in the inversion exponential is immaterial because the integrand
585	  pairs evenly under $r\mapsto-r$. Since $p_{2a}^{(1)}$ has mass one and $0 \le
586	  g_h \le 1/2$, we obtain $0 \le I_a(h,v) \le \pi/2$. Integrating against
587	  $\sigma$, whose mass is $V$, proves~\eqref{E:alpha-one-convolution}. This
588	  retains the oscillation until the one-dimensional integral is evaluated; the
589	  divergent absolute Fourier envelope at $\alpha = 1$ is not used. This proves
590	  Lemma~\ref{L:alpha-one-convolution}.
591	\end{proof}

696	\begin{corollary}[First-moment calibration]\label{C:d1-first-calibration}
697	  Let $K_*$ be $K_{\rm sp}$ under~\eqref{E:d1-covariances}, or $K_{\rm sp}^{\rm
698	  gen}$ under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{P:low-alpha-upper}. Put
699	  $C_{2,*} = q(2ZK_*)^{1/q}$. Then
700	  \begin{equation}\label{E:d1-first-calibration}
701	    \E u(t,x)\le\exp(C_{1,*}t^\kappa),\qquad
702	    C_{1,*}=q\left(\frac{ZK_*}{2^{3-\alpha}}\right)^{1/q}
703	    =\frac{C_{2,*}}{2^{(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha)}}.
704	  \end{equation}
705	  In either nonzero case $2C_{1,*} < C_{2,*}$. Conditionally on a first-moment
706	  lower rate at least $L_*$, $2L_* \le 2C_{1,*} < C_{2,*}$, consistently with
707	  Proposition~\ref{P:Jensen}.
708	\end{corollary}
709	
710	\begin{proof}
711	  For one chain of length $2k$, the increments sum to at most $t$. The spatial
712	  estimate in Lemma~\ref{L:d1-spatial}, or in the proof of
713	  Proposition~\ref{P:low-alpha-upper}, therefore applies with $t/2$ in place of
714	  $t$. The temporal pairing sum on one ordered simplex is
715	  $P_k(Zt^{2-\alpha_0})^k/(2k)!$. Using the same regularization and limit order
716	  as in the respective upper-bound proof gives
717	  \[
718	    \E X_{2k}(t,x)
719	    \le\frac{(ZK_*/2^{b+1})^k t^{\beta k}}{k!\,k^{bk}}
720	    \le\frac{(ZK_*/2^{3-\alpha})^k t^{\beta k}}{(k!)^q}.
721	  \]
722	  Every odd term has zero expectation. The $L^2$ expansion permits taking
723	  expectations of partial sums, and the resulting nonnegative even series is
724	  summed by the scalar inequality in the proof of Proposition~\ref{P:d1-upper}.
725	  This gives~\eqref{E:d1-first-calibration}. If the first-moment lower rate is
726	  at least $L_*$, \eqref{E:d1-first-calibration} implies $L_* \le C_{1,*}$. In
727	  the stated nonzero cases $K_* > 0$, hence $C_{1,*} > 0$; and
728	  $(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha) > 1$ gives $2C_{1,*} < C_{2,*}$. This proves
729	  Corollary~\ref{C:d1-first-calibration}.

820	  $\xi$, such that

830	  pushforward under $\lambda \mapsto \eta = \xi-\lambda$. Then $\nu_\xi(B(0,R))

1233	
1234	Write $E_r^{\mathrm{real}}$ for the real phase space in dimension $d$.
1235	
1236	\begin{proposition}[Column and adjoint-column maps]\label{P:wave-square-columns}
1237	  On the same probability space there are deterministic bounded real linear maps
1238	  \[
1239	    m_{R,I},n_{R,I}:E_{s-\gamma}^{\mathrm{real}}\longrightarrow
1240	    L^2(\Omega;E_s^{\mathrm{real}}),
1241	  \]
1242	  with squared bounds $C_T h^{2-a}B_\alpha(h)$, such that, for every fixed real
1243	  Schwartz pair $z,w$,
1244	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variance-square-columns}
1245	    \langle m_{R,I}z,w\rangle_E
1246	    = \ell_R(I;z,w) = \langle z,n_{R,I}w\rangle_E
1247	    \quad\text{in }L^2(\Omega).
1248	  \end{equation}
1249	  Fixed-vector values and finite families of values are centered Gaussian.
1250	\end{proposition}
1251	
1252	\begin{proof}
1253	  Choose a countable real Schwartz orthonormal basis $\{e_k\}$ of $E_s$. Such a
1254	  basis follows by Gram--Schmidt from a countable dense Schwartz family,
1255	  discarding zero residuals. Schwartz density follows by smooth Fourier cutoff
1256	  approximation in the weighted $L^2$ norms: approximate by compact smooth
1257	  Fourier coordinates, replace $g(\xi)$ by $(g(\xi)+\overline{g(-\xi)})/2$, and
1258	  apply the inverse Bessel/Fourier maps. The resulting phases are real Schwartz,
1259	  and Gram--Schmidt preserves that class. The same density holds in
1260	  $E_{s-\gamma}$.
1261	
1262	  For fixed real Schwartz $z$, define
1263	  \[
1264	    m_N(z) = \sum_{k\le N}\ell_R(I;z,e_k)e_k,
1265	    \qquad n_N(z) = \sum_{k\le N}\ell_R(I;e_k,z)e_k.
1266	  \]
1267	  Both are finite Gaussian sums on the original $W$. By
1268	  Proposition~\ref{P:wave-two-variances}, their coefficient expected squares
1269	  have finite sum. Orthogonality gives the squared tail norms as the
1270	  corresponding sums of expected squares. Thus, both sequences converge in
1271	  $L^2(\Omega;E_s)$ to $m(z),n(z)$ with the asserted bounds, without
1272	  independence of the coefficients. Finite-sum measurability and separable $E_s$
1273	  give strong measurability of the limits. The bounded real linear maps extend
1274	  uniquely from Schwartz phases to $E_{s-\gamma}$.
1275	
1276	  If $w_N$ is the $E_s$ projection of a Schwartz $w$ onto the first $N$ basis
1277	  vectors, then $\langle m_N(z),w\rangle_E = \ell_R(I;z,w_N)$. The singleton
1278	  form of~\eqref{E:wave-output-variance}, after normalizing $w-w_N$ in $E_s$,
1279	  gives
1280	  \[
1281	    \E|\ell_R(I;z,w-w_N)|^2
1282	    \le C_T h^{2-a}B_\alpha(h)\|z\|_{E_{s-\gamma}}^2\|w-w_N\|_{E_s}^2.
1283	  \]
1284	  The zero residual is immediate. The right side tends to zero, giving the first
1285	  identity in~\eqref{E:variance-square-columns}. For the second, project $z$
1286	  instead and use the singleton input bound \eqref{E:wave-input-variance}. A
1287	  fixed countable Schwartz orthonormal basis and Parseval show basis
1288	  independence of the constructed limits.
1289	
1290	  Continuous linear functionals of the limits, and finite linear combinations of
1291	  such functionals, are $L^2$ limits of centered Gaussian variables with
1292	  convergent variances. Their characteristic functions therefore converge to
1293	  those of centered Gaussians. The same reasoning after the bounded input
1294	  extension proves joint Gaussianity for arbitrary fixed inputs and finite
1295	  families of the two maps. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:wave-square-columns}.
1296	\end{proof}
